newsitem.title: CHINA: ASIA WEEK AHEAD-Stocks seen cautious on U.S. data.
newsitem.headline: ASIA WEEK AHEAD-Stocks seen cautious on U.S. data.

text.p: Caution is likely to be the watchword for regional stocks in the week ahead as investors watch domestic factors and any fallout from U.S. economic data.
Wall Street closed mostly lower on Friday with investors getting shocks from sharp increases in U.S. payrolls and manufacturing activity.

Although a late recovery all but erased an earlier fall of 119 points of the Dow Jones industrial average, analysts pointed to the heavy early losses as evidence that the market is ill-prepared to withstand any nasty surprises.

In Asia, currency factors and corporate earnings outlook could add to the uncertain mood, especially for the Thai, Philippine and Indonesian markets where recent de facto devaluations of the baht, peso and rupiah continue to be felt.
TOKYO - Stocks are expected to be range-bound in the week ahead with a small handful of high-tech issues underpinning the market, brokers said.

"Stocks tumbled on Friday and it remains to be seen if public funds step in to hunt for bargains," said a fund manager at a foreign investment trust. "If bargain hunting doesn't appear, the indices are likely to hover within a narrow range, only the range will be lower than in the past few weeks."

The Nikkei 225 had its sixth-largest point drop on news that domestic car sales fell for the fourth straight month year-on-year, indicating the economy was not recovering as hoped. The index ended down 527.05 points, or 2.59 percent, at 19,804.38, its first close below 20,000 since July 11 when it ended at 19,875.49.

"The fall on Friday was due largely to extraordinary reasons and does not necessarily mean that the Nikkei average has entered a down trend," said Hideyuki Ohkoshi, of Yamaichi Securities. "Support is seen at the July 9 low of 19,495.85."
HONG KONG - The Hang Seng is likely to head for a brief consolidation in the coming week after record gains, but the underlying tone remains positive, brokers said.
"This rally is led by properties, and the laggards in the sector and property developers should continue to see buyers," said Charles Cheung, executive director at J&A Securities.

Brokers said properties had largely lagged behind recent market gains and investors were buying on hopes that local property prices would bottom out soon after the government said there was no need at present to take measures against speculators.
On Friday, the Hang Seng index ended at 16,379.22, up 13.51 points, or 0.08 percent, after earlier touching an intra-day high of 16,449.53.

BANGKOK - The Thai market is expected to drop in the week ahead on negative factors including concerns about second quarter corporate earnings, talks between Thailand and the International Monetary Fund, and Standard & Poor's Corp's issuance of a negative creditwatch on Thailand.
"No positive news is seen at all. Investors are expected to pay attention to these negative factors and the index is expected to fall," said Samart Rusmeerojwong of James Capel Asia.
The Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) index gained 0.84 percent in the week to 652.04 points on Friday from a week earlier. It lost 2.04 percent from Thursday.
Brokers said they expected corporate earnings in the second quarter, due to be released later this month, would fare badly and they would have an impact on the market.
Results of talks with the IMF on ways to resolve Thailand's economic crisis were expected to be known on Tuesday when Finance Minister Thanong Bidaya presents them to the weekly cabinet meeting.
TAIPEI - Taiwan's red hot stock market is expected to continue to rise in the week ahead, with brokers saying the bull run may not end until the index breaches its all-time high of 12,495.34.
The market focus will remain on electronics, Taiwan's economic bellwether, backed by widespread expectations of a rise in fourth-quarter sales.
"The market still has momentum to rise, although the pace may be a bit slower," said Allen Huang, fund manager for National Securities.
The index closed on Saturday at 10,048.90 points, up 0.47 percent.
Taiwan's government was expected to release figures for the July consumer price index on Tuesday and trade data on Thursday.
A 10,000-10,500 range was seen for the coming week.
SEOUL - Seoul stocks are likely to fluctuate in a tight range in the coming week with selective bargain hunting alternating with selling on jitters over corporate crises, brokers said.
"The uncertain future of Kia will continue to haunt and investors would prefer to wait until the future becomes more clear," said Kim Ik-hwan of Hyundai Securities.
Creditor banks on Friday failed to make a decision on bailing out the troubled Kia Group because of continuing disagreements with management.
The composite index closed 730.43 on Saturday, little changed from last Saturday's 732.32.
JAKARTA - Indonesian stocks are likely to be mixed in the coming week as investors wait for the rupiah to further stabilise and more positive corporate news, brokers said.
"Many issuers and investors had lowered their expectations due to the general election last May," a senior analyst with local firm said.
On Friday, the Jakarta Composite Index closed at 721.77 points against 724.00 points the week before. The index was down 2.23 points, or 0.31 percent, on the week.
MANILA - Philippine shares are seen confined to a tight range over the coming week with mixed company earnings and a still edgy currency market, traders said.

"We see a range of 2,600 to 2,700. Currency volatility will still be a concern. But as long as there are no major earnings disappointments, we see the market inching up slightly," said Francisco Trinidad, research head at DBS Securities Phils.
The main index closed higher for the fifth straight day on Friday, rising 19.24 points to 2,635.64. Week-on-week, the index was up 62.95 points from the previous 2,572.69.

KUALA LUMPUR - Analysts said the Malaysian market was likely to fall below 1,000 points in the week ahead due to a lack of positive news, the continued absence of foreign funds and rumours of a big deficit in the June trade data.
Immediate support for the index is pegged at 980, analysts said.

For the week, the Composite Index of 100 large-capitalised stocks closed at 1,002.63, down 38.92 points, or 3.74 percent, from the previous week and down 10.21 points, or 1.01 percent, from Thursday's close.
SYDNEY - Australian shares are seen treading water near term with all eyes on the coming profit season.
"I can't see any broad issues to push it (the index) along. We will be waiting for the results to emerge," said a dealer at a Sydney-based investment bank.

The market finished the week in choppy trade with no clear trend as brokers dealt mainly two way business in modest turnover. The All Ordinaries index closed at 2,727.5, down 0.3 percent on the day, but up 1.3 percent on the week.

SINGAPORE - Dealers predicted bargain hunting in the coming week, possibly bringing in some foreign funds to spread positions after the record highs in Hong Kong and a slight consolidation in the United States.

"I expect to see some funds flowing back into small cap stocks next week. Singapore is priced for value at the moment," said one dealer with an international firm. "We could be a nice alternative to the U.S. and Hong Kong."
The Straits Times Industrials Index ended Friday at 1,955.25, down 25.71 on the previous week's close of 1,980.96.
WELLINGTON - The New Zealand market reached its highest level since before the 1987 crash on Wednesday and closed bullish on Friday, which brokers said augured well for the week ahead.
Nigel Scott at BZW said the market was very liquid, and any pull-backs following the strong rally had been on relatively low volume.
"I think we will continue to focus on our interest rates and currency -- that is what's really driving the markets at this point in time," he said.
The kiwi dollar has fallen sharply against the greenback recently, partly on the expectation of an easing of monetary policy by the Reserve Bank.
The NZSE-40 Capital Index closed the week at 2,574.63, up 172.1 points, or 7.16 percent, from its 2,402.53 close last week.
BOMBAY - Indian shares are expected to consolidate their gains in the coming week with the focus on domestic institutional demand, brokers said.
They said the Unit Trust of India, the country's largest mutual fund, has collected about 20 billion rupees in July and the money could start flowing into the market soon.
"The outlook is positive. I expect domestic institutional participation to supplement foreign fund buying," broker Maulik Sharedalal said.
In the week to Friday, the benchmark 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange index jumped 157.51 points, or 3.76 percent, to 4,347.32.

KARACHI - Pakistani stocks are likely to dip on a correction in the week ahead after a recent swift rise in the index, but dealers said sentiment would remain positive as second tier stocks attract investors' interest.

"A technical correction is now due as the market needs a breather after recent gains in active blue chips," a dealer said. "But local and foreign buying interest has now spilled over to second tier stocks as well and the index would hover at the current levels."
On Friday, the index ended down 56.25 points, or 2.83 percent, at 1,933.26 from 2,011.57 points on July 25.
